verdicts.summary: Reproducible epithelial rise, but no functional or genetic evidence and an intracellular enzyme with an amber drug route.

reasons.text: The rise is robust and epithelial, yet the only paper names it in a list and the target has no extracellular part; a first year of work would be a pure discovery bet.

verdicts.summary: Robust epithelial rise, but located in crypt cells that may be a repair programme, so inhibition could impair healing.

reasons.text: Its signal sits 94% in the crypt zone and rises there (amber cell light); organoid work must include a wound-healing read-out before any claim of benefit.

verdicts.summary: Fibroblast-made secreted protein with a clear antibody route, but 41% of the bulk rise is composition and nothing links it to function.

reasons.text: Genetic test is null and literature is one expression paper; a blocking antibody test is cheap, but the case rests on expression alone.

verdicts.summary: Secreted BMP antagonist: blocking it would raise BMP signalling, and the producing cell (fibroblast or smooth muscle) is unsettled.

reasons.text: Only 28% of the rise survives adjustment and its baseline marks severity in both drug and placebo arms; direction of benefit is unproven.

verdicts.summary: Best-documented candidate: epithelial, intrinsic rise, protein up, two mouse knockdown studies protective; tumour-suppressor concern is debatable.

reasons.text: Human IBD tissue studies found maspin overexpressed in active IBD and colitis-associated neoplasia and proposed targeting it, which tempers the tumour-suppressor safety concern.
reasons.claim: UniProt describes it as a tumour suppressor
reasons.quote: Targeting maspin for control of disease activity and cancer prophylaxis may be a promising novel therapeutic strategy for IBD.

reasons.text: Both mouse studies are 2026 and unreplicated, so organoid replication in human cells remains the right first step.

verdicts.summary: Neutrophil chemokine with a mouse literature of 69 papers; most of its rise is cell influx and the first experiment is sensible.

reasons.text: Chemokine blockade acting on neutrophil recruitment risks infection; the card correctly states that the circuit is co-expression only.

verdicts.summary: Strong marker, but knockout mice develop worse colitis, so inhibition may harm epithelium; marker first, target second.

reasons.text: Functional studies point in both directions and vital-organ expression is high (424 nTPM); the parallel fibroblast and organoid test is appropriate.

verdicts.summary: Epithelial regenerating-crypt gene with biomarker papers only and no functional study; blocking it may slow repair.

reasons.text: Direction is unproven: it may be a repair programme to restore rather than inhibit, so a gain- and loss-of-function test is the right first step.

verdicts.summary: Activin A inhibition has mouse colitis support, but the approved drug is a ligand trap with broad effects and the gene is strongly constrained.

reasons.text: Activin blockade with follistatin attenuated DSS colitis and preserved epithelium in mice, which supports the inhibit direction; the card says it was never tested in mouse colitis.
reasons.quote: Importantly, in vivo administration of follistatin attenuated inflammatory cell infiltration during colitis.

reasons.text: Constraint (LOEUF 0.17) and a drug that traps several activin and GDF ligands make safety and selectivity the main caveats.

verdicts.summary: Approved factor B inhibitor makes this practical, but a protective loss-of-function variant and complement-deficiency risk argue against.

reasons.text: A red safety light, a protective variant in Crohn's disease and no response signal make this a test of harm as much as of benefit; mucosal host defence is the concern.

verdicts.summary: P-selectin blockade has been tried in experimental colitis without benefit, and the gene is only a local-inflammation signal.

reasons.text: Anti-P-selectin antibody blocked leukocyte rolling but did not significantly improve TNBS colitis in rats.
reasons.claim: First experiment: the existing antibody in a flow assay
reasons.quote: However, treatment with an anti-P-selectin antibody does not significantly improve colitis.

reasons.text: Null Mendelian randomisation and non-responder separation in both arms add to the case against testing it first.

verdicts.summary: Plausible innate target with an eritoran route, but neutrophil influx and a possible healing defect complicate it.

reasons.text: Much of the rise reports cell arrival and another TLR4/MD-2 antibody impaired recovery; the proposed early and recovery readings address this.

verdicts.summary: Genetics support is real, but the gene is a ubiquitous mitochondrial factor, biopsies show no rise, and the predicted cell does not match.

reasons.text: A mitochondrial translation factor cannot be inhibited broadly; cell-specific delivery, a single instrument and no tissue change make it a poor first-year bet.

verdicts.summary: Transcription factor with a tissue rise and a drug-like lead, but the Mendelian signal points the other way and the cell source is mixed.

reasons.text: Broadly expressed in neutrophils and macrophages, hard to drug, and predicted in a minor cell type; it is a hypothesis for later.

verdicts.summary: Only a sequence prediction in NK cells: no Mendelian support, no biopsy change, no drug route.

reasons.text: The card itself says it stays only to fill the list; I would not spend a year on it.

verdicts.summary: Only a sequence prediction in goblet cells: no Mendelian support, no biopsy change, no drug route.

reasons.text: Confirming the variant's effect on expression is a sensible check, but not a reason to prioritise it as a target.

objections.claim: UniProt describes it as a tumour suppressor, so long-term inhibition in a colon at risk of cancer needs care
objections.objection: Human IBD tissue data show maspin overexpressed in active IBD and in colitis-associated neoplasia, which weakens the tumour-suppressor safety argument; the cancer effect is unsettled.
objections.suggestion: Reword to say the tumour-suppressor role in the colon is unsettled, as maspin is overexpressed in IBD-associated neoplasia.
objections.quote: Targeting maspin for control of disease activity and cancer prophylaxis may be a promising novel therapeutic strategy for IBD.

objections.claim: First experiment: the existing inhibitor on inflamed UC fibroblasts and macrophages, then on explants of inflamed mucosa.
objections.objection: The card omits that activin blockade with follistatin already attenuated DSS colitis in mice, the only colitis evidence for the gene's direction, which an expert would want stated.
objections.suggestion: State that mouse colitis data exist for activin blockade.
objections.quote: Importantly, in vivo administration of follistatin attenuated inflammatory cell infiltration during colitis.

objections.claim: First experiment: the existing antibody in a flow assay of neutrophils over inflamed UC endothelial cells.
objections.objection: The text omits that anti-P-selectin antibody did not significantly improve TNBS colitis in rats despite blocking rolling; without it the decision misleads about expected benefit.
objections.suggestion: State the negative colitis result among the points against the gene.
